source_text:
High–entropy alloys (HEAs) have had remarkable progress and advancement since their development by Professor Yeh in 2004. The term “high–entropy alloy” generally refers to a single–phase solid solution alloy with a simple crystal structure composed of five or more elements, with an atomic percentage ranging from 5% to 35%. Given their superior hardness, exceptional strength, resistance to corrosion, and a multitude of additional benefits, HEAs have became a new type of alloy material that has received a great deal of attention in the research field during recent years and the hot point of many researches. The high–entropy alloy composed of five elements–Cobalt (Co), Chromium (Cr), Iron (Fe), Nickel (Ni), and Titanium (Ti)–in equimolar or nearly equimolar proportions exhibited a simple solid solution structure and favorable plasticity and machinability. However, it suffered from a relatively low hardness and strength. The existing research lacked a comprehensive and thorough understanding of the microstructure and deformation dynamics of the CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloy.

High–entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibit remarkable properties, such as exceptional strength coupled with ductility, elevated strength at high temperatures, thermal stability, corrosion resistance, and notable electrical resistance. There are four ways to fabricate HEAs: melting, gas–phase synthesis, electrochemical techniques, and solid–state processing. Among these, casting worked as the predominant method employed for HEA production. However, the casting process is fraught with challenges. During solidification, thermal expansion and contraction occur, giving rise to numerous structural imperfections, notably porosity. Consequently, the microstructure resulting from solidification is far from homogeneous. This non–uniformity in the microstructure can subsequently lead to heterogeneous material properties, which may compromise the alloy’s performance in certain applications. Mechanical alloying, a solid–phase manufacturing technique, facilitates the production of high–entropy alloys (HEAs) with homogeneity superior to that of the casting method. Given its efficacy in generating solid solutions, mechanical alloying enables the synthesis of nanostructured HEAs. Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS), a technique that uses electric current to trigger the consolidation and reaction sintering processes of materials, offers distinct benefits when compared to time–consuming conventional methods such as hot pressing, hot isostatic sintering, high–frequency induction heating, isostatic pressing and sintering (a combination process), hot isostatic pressing (the repeated mention here is for clarity in contrasting with SPS), and liquid phase sintering. It enables substantial material compaction at relatively low temperatures and within a shorter timeframe. Zeraati M  reported an AlCrCuFeNiTi HEA synthesized through MA, followed by consolidation using SPS. The mechanical properties of the consolidated sample were remarkable, featuring a yield stress of 2004 MPa, a compressive strength of 2811 MPa, and a Vickers hardness of 684 HV. Adabavazeh, Z  focused on the fabrication and assessment of a CuFeNiMnTi HEA, synthesized via MA and SPS. The sintered CuFeNiMnTi alloy exhibited a fracture toughness of 9.24 ± 0.5 MPa root at room temperature, along with significant mechanical enhancements, including a microhardness of 563 ± 22 HVN and an Ultimate Shear Strength (USS) of 439 ± 19 MPa. Yurchenko, N  reported low–density AlCrFeTiX (where X = Co, Ni, Cu) high–entropy alloys made using MA and SPS. Compression testing revealed that the SPS–processed AlCrFeTiX (X = Co, Ni, Cu) alloys exhibited brittle behavior at room temperature (25 °C). At an elevated temperature of 600 °C, the SPS–processed AlCrFeTiCo alloy exhibited a yield strength of 1960 MPa, a peak strength of 2121 MPa, and a plastic strain of 1.8%. These alloys exhibited remarkable properties, including elevated hardness and outstanding compressive performance.

queries.broad: For high-entropy alloys, what single intervention could improve hardness and strength without sacrificing useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, the mechanism expected to produce the improvement, a measurable outcome relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with clear observations that would falsify it.
queries.problem_constrained: An equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy has a simple solid-solution structure and favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength, while its microstructure and deformation behavior remain insufficiently understood. Under hardness testing and mechanical loading of this starting state, what single intervention could overcome the strength and hardness limitation while retaining its favorable mechanical characteristics? State the proposed intervention, its mechanism, the predicted measurable change relative to the unmodified alloy, its applicable processing and test conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a microstructural and mechanical experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.
queries.expert_context: Casting is the predominant high-entropy-alloy fabrication method, but solidification-related porosity and microstructural nonuniformity can produce heterogeneous properties. Prior studies of other HEA compositions used mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering and reported high hardness and compressive strength; however, these results do not establish a solution for CoCrFeNiTi, and one reported alloy family remained brittle at 25 °C and showed only limited plastic strain at 600 °C. For equimolar or nearly equimolar, simple-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi—which has favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength—what single intervention could improve hardness and strength while preserving those favorable characteristics and enabling clearer understanding of its microstructure–deformation relationship? Provide the intervention, the proposed mechanism, a quantitative prediction relative to the untreated starting alloy, the processing and testing boundaries within which it should apply, the prior evidence that supports it, and a controlled microstructural and mechanical experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

leaks.phrase: mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering
leaks.why: This explicitly names the same intervention class and processing sequence as the hidden answer: high-energy ball milling/mechanical alloying followed by SPS. Although framed as prior work on other HEAs, it strongly cues the proposed treatment for CoCrFeNiTi.
